strengths: Addresses practical and important problem of data-efficient humanoid robot learning with real-world validation on LimX Ohi robot
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with systematic ablation studies examining training time proportion, data proportion, and different SRL method choices
Well-structured methodology with clear formulation; intuitive use of contrastive learning between proprioceptive and privileged states
Provides actionable insights about when SRL helps (important for motion imitation, less critical for velocity tracking) with quantitative evidence
SRL4Humanoid framework contribution unifying multiple SRL implementations that could benefit the community
Computational efficiency analysis demonstrates feasibility of SRL methods with minimal overhead
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing contrastive learning techniques to robot domain rather than introducing fundamentally new methods
Modest empirical improvements, especially for velocity tracking where differences between PvP and PPO+SPR/SimSiam are small; final performance gains are incremental
Real-world validation is mostly qualitative (Figure 11 shows poses) without quantitative metrics comparing PvP vs baselines on actual robot; no real-world ablations
Narrow experimental scope with only 2 tasks and 1 robot platform; generalizability claims are overstated
Insufficient baseline comparisons: limited to PPO+SRL variants with no comparison to other state-of-the-art humanoid control methods (diffusion policies, transformers, behavior cloning)
Weak theoretical justification for why contrastive learning is specifically superior to other auxiliary losses for leveraging privileged information
Unresolved stability issues evident in training collapse (Figure 10) when applying SRL to value encoder; interval update mechanism (Eq. 6) lacks principled justification

Missing critical ablations: no analysis of contrastive loss design choices, scaling with privileged information dimensionality, or failure modes; inconsistent VAE underperformance not adequately explained
Important experimental details and hyperparameter search methodology relegated to appendices; unclear if all methods received uniform tuning; code availability not confirmed at submission
Ad-hoc design choices without principled justification (e.g., zero-masking operation in Eq. 2, why negative cosine similarity, scheduling strategy for SRL contribution)

strengths: Addresses important practical problem in humanoid robot learning with a well-motivated approach combining privileged information and contrastive learning

Comprehensive experimental validation including systematic ablation studies, simulation experiments on velocity tracking and motion imitation tasks, and real-robot demonstrations on the LimX Oii humanoid
SRL4Humanoid framework is a valuable open-source contribution providing high-quality, modular implementations of multiple SRL methods, beneficial for the research community
Thorough analysis of different factors affecting learning (training time proportion, data proportion, update intervals, weighting coefficients) offering practical insights
Includes real-world robot experiments beyond simulation, demonstrating practical applicability and motion imitation capabilities on actual hardware
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core idea is a relatively straightforward combination of existing concepts (privileged states + contrastive learning) without significant methodological innovations

Mixed and inconsistent experimental results: PvP shows clear improvements on velocity tracking but modest/inconsistent gains on motion imitation; VAE sometimes matches or exceeds PvP, and the paper inadequately explains these discrepancies or their implications for task generalization

Real-robot validation is primarily qualitative (visual demonstrations in Figure 11) without quantitative comparisons between methods on actual hardware, undermining claims about practical effectiveness

Insufficient theoretical justification: lack of rigorous analysis for why PvP should work, the 'intrinsic complementarity' claim needs deeper support, and design choices (e.g., Eq. 4 formulation, privileged state for value encoder) lack clear motivation

Narrow task evaluation: experiments limited to relatively simple, constrained scenarios (flat-terrain velocity tracking, pre-recorded motion imitation); acknowledged limitations with terrain variation and external disturbances suggest limited scope

Incomplete baseline comparisons: only compared against vanilla PPO + SRL methods; missing comparisons with recent data-efficient RL approaches, model-based methods, other privileged information techniques, or state-of-the-art humanoid control methods

Unclear design choices and justifications: zero-masking operation, hyperparameter selections appear arbitrary, and the scheduling mechanism (Eq. 6) seems ad-hoc; some design rationales only explained post-hoc

Statistical rigor concerns: unclear number of random seeds, some reported improvements appear within standard deviation ranges, and limited discussion of statistical significance despite shown error bars
